opus-5.5.text:
I think infrastructure is probably the single biggest variable in that timeline, maybe even bigger than the model architecture itself.

If you look back at language models, the path from GPT-1 to ChatGPT took roughly four or five years. But that path ran on infrastructure that was already there. The internet had been accumulating text for decades. GPUs were maturing. The software stack for distributed training was getting better. So when people found the right recipe, scaling was mostly an engineering problem. You could just pour in more data and more compute.

Robotics doesn't have that luxury yet. We don't have an "internet of physical interaction." Every trajectory, every grasp, every failure has to be collected somehow, through teleoperation, simulation, or human videos. Each of those has its own problems. Teleoperation is expensive and slow. Simulation has the sim-to-real gap. Human video lacks action labels and the embodiment is different. So right now, I'd say a lot of the field is still in the stage of building the pipes rather than running water through them.

Hardware is another layer of infrastructure people underestimate. In language, the "body" is basically a tokenizer. Everyone shares it. In robotics, every lab has different arms, different grippers, different sensors, different control frequencies. Data collected on one platform doesn't transfer cleanly to another. Until there's some convergence, or until models become good enough at cross-embodiment generalization, data won't compound the way it did for text.

So my honest view is that the timeline from a robot GPT-1 to a robot ChatGPT could be longer than it was for language, unless infrastructure catches up quickly. But I'm also optimistic, because this is exactly where a lot of investment is going now: large-scale data collection factories, better simulators, world models that can generate training data, and more standardized hardware. If those pieces mature together, things could accelerate very suddenly. That's what happened in language, too. It looked slow until it suddenly wasn't.

One more thing: I'm not sure "robot ChatGPT" will look like a single moment. ChatGPT was a product breakthrough as much as a technical one. It found the right interface for people to feel the capability. For robots, the equivalent might be a specific scenario, maybe in the home, maybe in logistics, where the robot is good enough, reliable enough, and cheap enough that people suddenly get it. Reaching that point depends not only on the model but on the whole system around it. That's why I keep coming back to infrastructure.

r001.rationale: The response says language-model progress benefited from infrastructure that was already in place, making scaling mostly an engineering problem.

r002.rationale: The response says the robotics timeline could be longer than the language timeline unless infrastructure catches up; it does not suggest the robot progression may take less time.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because the honest answer is that infrastructure is probably the biggest variable in that timeline, more than the algorithms themselves.

If you look back at language models, the path from GPT-1 to ChatGPT took roughly four years, and a huge part of why it moved that fast was that the infrastructure was already there. The internet had spent twenty years accumulating text. GPUs had been optimized for dense matrix computation because of gaming and then deep learning for vision. Distributed training frameworks existed. So when the scaling recipe became clear, people could just pour resources in and the system responded.

Robotics today is in a very different position. We don't have the equivalent of the internet for physical interaction data. Every robot in the world collects data on different hardware, with different sensors, different action spaces, different frequencies. Even if you gathered all of it, you'd have a messy, fragmented dataset that's orders of magnitude smaller than what language models trained on. So the first bottleneck is simply that the data infrastructure doesn't exist yet, and it has to be built from scratch, often by the same people trying to build the models.

The second thing is that the hardware loop is slow. In language, your iteration cycle is bounded by compute. You run an experiment, you get a result, you adjust. In robotics, you're bounded by the physical world. A robot can only do one thing at a time, in real time. If you want a million trajectories of a robot folding laundry, that is a million real episodes somewhere, with real failures, real repairs, real humans supervising. Simulation helps, and I'm actually fairly optimistic about simulation and world models closing part of that gap, but the sim-to-real transfer problem hasn't been fully solved, so you can't rely on it the way language models rely on scraped text.

Then there's the deployment side, which people underestimate. ChatGPT could reach a hundred million users in two months because the delivery infrastructure was a web browser. A robot ChatGPT needs the robot. That means manufacturing, supply chains, cost reduction, safety certification. Even if the model were ready tomorrow, getting it into millions of homes or factories is a hardware problem that moves at hardware speed.

So my view is that today's infrastructure will stretch the timeline, not shorten it. I don't think it will be a four-year jump like language. But I also think there's a flywheel waiting to start. Once there are enough robots deployed doing real tasks, they generate data, the data improves the model, the better model justifies more deployment. The companies that win will be the ones who treat data collection and hardware as first-class infrastructure, not as something separate from the research. We're in the phase of laying the pipes right now, and that phase is slow and unglamorous, but it's the thing that eventually lets everything else accelerate.

r001.rationale: The response says existing infrastructure—accumulated text, optimized GPUs, and distributed training frameworks—helped language models progress quickly once the scaling recipe was clear.

r002.rationale: The response says robotics infrastructure will stretch the timeline and that it will not be a four-year jump like language models, implying a longer progression rather than a shorter one.

astra-6.text:
I think today’s infrastructure could make that timeline much shorter, but there’s still a big uncertainty around data. We’re not starting from scratch: we already have powerful models, computing infrastructure, and tools for training and deploying them. A robot can build on those capabilities rather than having to learn everything about the world through physical interaction.

But robotics has a different bottleneck. With language, you can train on enormous amounts of existing text. With robots, you need examples of actions and their consequences, and collecting those examples in the real world is slower and more expensive. You also need the system to work reliably across different environments, objects, and hardware.

So I’m optimistic that we can move quickly from an early general-purpose robot model to something genuinely useful. What’s harder to predict is when we get a ChatGPT-like moment—when ordinary people can ask a robot to do a wide range of tasks and expect it to succeed. Today’s infrastructure gives us a substantial head start, but the pace will depend on how quickly we can build that cycle of deployment, data collection, and improvement.

r001.rationale: It says existing computing infrastructure and training tools let robotics build on current capabilities and give a “substantial head start,” clearly communicating that established infrastructure accelerates development.

r002.rationale: It says the timeline could be much shorter, but does not compare the robot progression with the original GPT-1-to-GPT-3.5 or ChatGPT progression.

sol-6.1.text:
I think today’s infrastructure could make that transition much faster, but robotics still has a different bottleneck. For language models, we already had enormous amounts of text on the internet. For robots, we don’t yet have an equivalent collection of diverse interactions with the physical world.

We can build on the compute, model architectures, and training tools developed for language and vision. A robot also doesn’t need to learn everything from scratch: pretrained models can provide useful visual and semantic understanding. That gives us a much stronger starting point.

But we still need to collect action data, make it useful across different robots, and evaluate whether a system can reliably complete tasks in unfamiliar environments. Physical deployment makes that loop slower: you have hardware failures, safety constraints, and experiments that take real time.

So I’d expect the software side to move quickly, while data collection and deployment determine the overall pace. The key question is whether we can create a loop where more deployed robots produce better data, better data improves the model, and that improvement enables more deployment. If that loop starts working, the transition could accelerate substantially. I’d be cautious about attaching a specific number of years to it.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics can build on compute, model architectures, and training tools developed for language and vision, giving it a stronger starting point and potentially speeding the transition.

r002.rationale: It says the robot transition could be faster, but does not compare its duration with the progression from the original GPT-1 to GPT-3.5 or ChatGPT.
